description.narrative: Det övergripande målet är att ungdomar och unga vuxna i östra och södra Afrika genom ökad egenmakt och motståndskraft, i ökad utsträckning engagerar sig, skapar nätverk och förbättrar sin sexuella och reproduktiva hälsa och rättigheter. Målet ska uppnås genom fyra övergripande outcomes; - Ökat regionalt ansvar för SRHR påskyndar medlemsländernas förverkligande av Agenda 2030 och SDG 3. - Attityder och handlingar bland rättighetsbärare, de som formar normer, och unga är i ökad grad stödjande av ungas SRHR - Unga tar en ökad roll i sin egen hälsa och i system för hälsa. - Förbättrad SRHR bland unga genom att komponenter av effektiva modeller för ungas SRHR genomförs.

The goal is to ensure that adolescents and young people in Eastern and Southern Africa with improved access to quality sexual and reproductive health and wellness services, enjoy increased health, agency, and resilience. This will be achieved through four main outcomes: - Increased regional accountability for SRHR accelerates member states' realisation of Agenda 2030 and SDG 3. - Growing support among targeted duty bearers, norms makers, and young people for adolescent sexual and reproductive health and rights (ASRHR), is reflected in their attitudes and actions. - Empowered and networked young people play an increased role in their own health and in systems for health. - Targeted implementation of effective ASRHR models in SADC members states improves adolescent health outcomes.

The overall goal of the AI Programme is that adolescents and young people in East and Southern Africa have improved access to quality sexual and reproductive health and wellness services, enjoy increased health, agency, and resilience.
The long term outcomes are as follow:
1. Increased regional accountability for SRHR accelerates member states realisation of Agenda 2063 and SDG 3 2. Growing support among targeted duty bearers, norms makers, and youngpeople for adolescent sexual and reproductive health and rights (ASRHR), reflected in their attitudes and actions 3. Empowered and networked young people play an increased role in their own health and in systems for health 4. Targeted implementation of effective ASRHR models in SADC member states improved adolescent health outcomes SAT intends to work with key stakeholders

title.narrative: Grant agreement between Sida and Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights Africa Trust

description.narrative:
During the reporting year of 2024, some of the results SAT reports against the long and medium term outcomes include:
LONGTERM RESULT 1: INCREASED REGIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY FOR SRHR ACCELERATES MEMBER STATES REALISATION OF AGENDA 2063 AND SDG 3 This longterm result area emphasises the development of progressive SRHR policies and laws, as well as ensuring accountability in the implementation of existing regulations and funding of SRHR within health financing & Universal Health Coverage (UHC). The LTR is realised through the active engagement of civil society organisations (CSOs) and young people with SRHR duty bearers, supported by SAT as an active party, a catalytic agent, or an interlocuter in engagements at international, regional, national, and local levels.
Mediumterm outcome 1.1: An increased number of civil society members, including young people, in the region engage meaningfully in key SRHR spaces, places and processes at all levels to shift SRHR policies, laws, and practices. The most significant progress marker under this mediumterm outcome was the Cotonou Youth Action Agenda (CYAA), a progressive vision for adolescent and youth health and development, extending beyond the ICPD plan of action (PoA). Before the UN Summit of the Future, the AI Programme sent a staff member to the global youth meeting in Cotonou, Benin. The staff member played a central role in coordinating youth and youth organisations, and together with the UN Major Group for Children and Youth (UN MGCY), drafted, consulted and facilitated the adoption of the Cotonou Youth Action Agenda (CYAA), a progressive vision for adolescent and youth health and development, extending beyond the ICPD plan of Action (PoA). As young people and their organisations prepare for a post 2030 agenda, the UN Major Group for Children and Youth is using the Cotonou Youth Action Agenda to spearhead the development of a new youth SRHR advocacy and accountability mobilisation initiative. This will convene youth-led organisations working on SRHR and build collective capacity to strategize and prepare towards the post-2030/SDG negotiations beginning in 2027 and is intended to ensure adolescent and young people's needs and priorities on their health, well-being and rights are at the forefront of negotiations.
Mediumterm outcome 1.2: Evidence generated is used to support shifts in policy, practice and accountability at regional and memberstate levels. A significant progress marker under this outcome was that in response to SAT Programme findings and advocacy, especially on glaring and critical data gaps, the National AIDS Health Promoting Agency (NAHPA) in Botswana engaged a team of experts from Statistics Botswana to assist with populating updated and accurate data within the Condoms Needs Estimation Tool (CNET). At last-mile levels, the experiences of the AI programme of tracking and moving commodities across local clinics when there are stock-outs influenced the Condom Programming Coordinator (responsible for both condom programming and adolescent girls and young women at the National AIDS Health Promoting Agency) to adopt a new commodity tracking and distribution strategy informed by the Condoms Needs Estimation Tool as opposed to the old central distribution (e.g. via District Health Management Teams) for implementation in 2025. This has already led to more demand-sensitive allocations and commodity supply security in the Greater Gaborone area.
Mediumterm outcome 1.3: SRHR and ASRHR-engaged civil society impact regional and member state health financing and UHC. A significant progress marker here was a dedicated budget line for Youth Friendly Health Services in the National Health Budget established for the first time in Malawi, securing an avenue for transparent allocations and accounting. In Malawi, the advocacy of the AI Programme in collaboration with other CSOs within the Universal Health Coverage Coalition and the Collaborative Advocacy Action Plan successfully led to an increase in the national budget allocation for health, from 8.4% in 2023/2024 to 12.9% in 2024/2025. Additionally, a dedicated budget line for Youth Friendly Health Services was established for the first time securing an avenue for transparent allocations and accounting.
LONGTERM OUTCOME 2: GROWING SUPPORT AMONG TARGETED DUTY BEARERS, NORMS MAKERS, AND YOUNG PEOPLE FOR ASRHR, REFLECTED IN THEIR ATTITUDES AND ACTIONS Under this long-term outcome, the AI programme aims to shape how communities, including young people, perceive and respond to SRHR issues. In 2024, the programme collaborated with gatekeepers, key enablers, young people, and nontraditional SRHR advocates to promote progressive social norms around ASRHR. .
Mediumterm outcome 2.1: Partnerships supporting ASRHR established with nontraditional SRHR allies and influential norms-making bodies and leaders. In Zimbabwe, in September 2024, the AI Programme convened a round table meeting to explore pathways for enhancing access to SRH services for young people through partnerships with nontraditional stakeholders. A key outcome was the establishment of a partnership with the National Prosecuting Authority to advocate for the review of age of consent legislation. Additionally, the partnership aims to develop referral pathways between the National Prosecuting Authority, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders to ensure adolescent and young people survivors of GBV or SRH related crimes receive comprehensive support and justice.
Mediumterm outcome 2.2: Increased public visibility of young people engaging in public spaces. The mediumterm outcome is aimed at increasing the acceptance of young people, and in particular adolescent girls and young women by creating opportunities for their public participation, and by supporting their capacity to participate meaningfully in those opportunities. Increasing public visibility has two components. Firstly, visibility among their peers in ways that create role models and spark inspiration for others to engage in activism. This has taken place via online interactions with young people through YouthWyze channels and via service delivery outreaches. In addition, SAT Youth Hub members appeared on 2 TV shows, 5 radio talk shows, at 3 regional high profile events 1 international conference, in addition to playing significant roles in 16 SRHR-related global days.
The second component of visibility, is in the eyes of older people, including duty bearers and traditional and faith leaders. This has been designed to be achieved over the Programme period and for outcome measurement it will need to include surveys and interviews to determine whether these crafted appearances are translating into changes of mind and greater acceptance of these roles. This measurement did not take place in 2023 or 2024. Rather, the Programme has up till now focused on the preparation and placement of young people in public spaces and processes.
LONGTERM RESULT 3: EMPOWERED AND NETWORKED YOUNG PEOPLE PLAY AN INCREASED ROLE IN THEIR OWN HEALTH AND IN SYSTEMS FOR HEALTH. This longterm outcome is concerned with enhancing adolescent agency and resilience to improve wellness and SRHR outcomes. In 2024 the AI programme sought to empower and connect young activists and young people in youth-led networks that facilitate exchange of knowledge and solutions about their health. The engine of this youth empowerment and networking was the five Youth Hubs and four Youth Hub alumni groups made up 376 members of which 256 (69%) were adolescent girls and young women members.
Mediumterm outcome 3.1: Increased collaboration on capacity and representation among young activists in a movement in and across countries to strengthen ASRHR in systems for health. Noteworthy collaborations for the year included in Malawi where, drawing on the 2022 Rapid Assessment of SRH, HIV, and AIDS services in higher education, which revealed that many students do not have access to SRHR, HIV and AIDS information and services, the AI programme teamed up with COMYODS (the Center for Community Health, Research, and Youth Development) to roll out handson, peer-to-peer training across several universities and colleges in Malawi. The Programme equipped 130 student volunteers from these institutions to serve as peer educators and distributors. They now confidently share accurate SRHR, HIV, and AIDS information, distribute condoms and emergency contraceptive pills, and connect their classmates with local health services.
Mediumterm outcome 3.2: Increased number of young people access SRHR education, information, counselling, and services. During the reporting period, the AI Programme contributed to YouthWyze distributing CSE messaging across 14 Countries in Southern, East, and West Africa via versions of the YouthWize App, WhatsApp messaging, social media, and via SAT country pages. Collectively these channels secured 226,153 unique followers. Post engagement on CSE for the year (the total number of times an individual reacted to the post/s by liking, sharing, commenting on the post, etc.) was 3,521,593.
LONGTERM RESULT 4: TARGETED IMPLEMENTATION OF EFFECTIVE ASRHR MODELS IN SADC MEMBER STATES IMPROVES ADOLESCENT HEALTH OUTCOMES. The AI programme has invested in approaches that foster collaborations and the delivery of quality health care and health outcomes for adolescents and young people in strengthening health systems.
Mediumterm outcome 4.1: Community-led monitoring by civil society provides grounded evidence for accountability for quality delivery of ASRHR. Data on SRH services availability, affordability, accessibility, and the quality of services were collected via mystery customer and exit questions from 68 adolescent-serving health facilities in 8 cities across 6 ESA member states (5 in SADC, and one in EAC). The mystery evaluation method involves having an individual pose a client and interact with the healthcare worker.
Evidence from community/youth-led monitoring exercises was used in engagements with health facility staff, district health management committees and heads of ministries of health in the four SADC states. In Malawi, the AI programme engaged Youth Hub members to assess and monitor service delivery of ASRHR services in 5 targeted Health centres in Lilongwe.
Mediumterm outcome 4.2: Selected components of adolescent-centred ASRHR are introduced with government support in targeted SADC member states. In September 2024, in collaboration with Youth Aspire Development Trust (YADT), the AI Programme launched a school health pilot project in the Chitungwiza district of Harare, Zimbabwe. The pilot demonstrated a significant demand for SRH information and services among students, including LGBTQI individuals. The programme successfully screened 500 learners and referred them to local health facilities and partner organisations that provide youth friendly SRH services. By the end of the year district support was evident for the Programme, and the Ministry of Education was informally in discussions with SAT about how these innovations might go national.
